catalog_quote: La fuente colonial parece presentar tres acentos: agudo, grave y circunflejo. El acento agudo recae en la posición final, salvo cuatro excepciones. Habría que pensar, por lo tanto, que era fijo en la última sílaba del tema. El acento grave, por otra parte, recae en la sílaba final; parece ser, en consecuencia, un acento fijo en dicha sílaba, por consiguiente, no distintivo. new_statements.translation: The colonial source seems to show three accents: acute, grave and circumflex. However, the latter must rather be an indication of vowel nasality (see 1.4.3); Albis, for his part, only includes the acute and grave accents. The acute accent falls in final position, save four exceptions. One would therefore have to think that it was fixed on the last syllable of the stem. The grave accent, for its part, falls on the final syllable; it seems, consequently, to be an accent fixed on that syllable, and therefore non-distinctive. [...] The grave-accent and acute-accent diacritics probably represented an accent fixed on the last syllable, which, being predictable, lacked phonemic value.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent fell on the final syllable (of the stem/word) and was predictable, hence non-contrastive; inferred from the placement of acute and grave accent marks in the 18th-century colonial wordlist and Albis's vocabulary.
new_statements.exceptions: Four items in the colonial source carry the acute accent on a non-final syllable (not listed in sec. 10); circumflex marks are reinterpreted as nasality, not accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about written citation forms in colonial-era vocabularies; author says 'última sílaba del tema' (last syllable of the stem) for the acute and 'sílaba final' for the grave, i.e. word/stem-final in isolated word forms. Philological inference from orthographic diacritics, not from speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Extinct language known only from an anonymous 18th-century colonial vocabulary (Real Biblioteca ms.) and Albis (1855/1860-61); Coronas Urzúa's statement is a philological interpretation of the accent diacritics in those written sources, not an observation of speech. Not to be confused with Andaqui as an ethnonym applied to Inga (Quechuan) speakers of the upper Caquetá.
